title: Fidelity ladder, tool fallthrough, and SDK handshake PRD (draft)
content:
Problem statement:
Teams building interactive, tool-enabled experiences want predictable, debuggable progressive output while keeping client SDKs simple. Today: streaming frames are either opaque text chunks or heavy, schema-first blobs. Tool calls surface separately and often require ad-hoc client-side glue. When a tool is slow or unavailable, apps either block the user or return inconsistent partial results.

Goal (short):
Design a pragmatic "fidelity ladder" for progressive streaming plus a small, ergonomic SDK handshake that:
- Provides progressively richer structured output levels clients can opt into.
- Defines consistent tool-call frames and a clear fallthrough policy for degraded capacity.
- Keeps SDK ergonomics simple for common patterns (chat + tools) while allowing power users to opt into typed streaming.
- Exposes telemetry hooks and health signals needed for rollout and SLOs.

Success criteria (measurable):
- 95% of prototype integrations can be implemented using <= 8 SDK calls and standard callbacks.
- Tool-related error or mismatch rate (schema mismatch, tool-timeout) < 1% after rollout phase.
- No worse than 10% median end-to-end latency increase for streaming baseline when fidelity ladder is enabled.
- Developer satisfaction score (qualitative) >= 4/5 in partner trials.

User personas:
- Frontend engineer: wants a thin API and predictable incremental UI updates for progressive results.
- Backend integration owner: needs reliable tool-call semantics and observability.
- SDK consumer (platform team): wants both default easy path and typed progressive outputs for complex workflows.

Principles and constraints:
- Backwards compatibility: default plain-stream behavior remains unchanged unless client opts into handshake.
- Incremental adoption: new protocol version negotiated at call start; fall back to v1 streaming when unknown.
- Minimal wire overhead: keep frames compact (small enums + length-prefixed payload).
- Server-driven degradation: server chooses fallthrough policy based on capacity and tool health; client receives reason codes.

Fidelity ladder (concept):
A small set of progressive fidelity levels that encode increasing structure and actionable content. Clients may subscribe to one or more levels at call start. Levels:
- L0: Raw incremental text (legacy streaming).
- L1: Coarse semantics (labels like "outline", "fact", "opinion") attached to text spans. Lightweight JSON lines.
- L2: Structured blocks (JSON objects) describing discrete units: summary blocks, code blocks, action candidates. Each block carries a stable id and sequence index.
- L3: Executable action frames for tool-calls: full typed payloads (method, args, expected return schema), preconditions, and recovery hints.
Clients should be able to request e.g., "L0+L2" to get both raw text and structured blocks.

Wire protocol (high-level):
- Client initiates a streaming call with headers: model, requested_fidelity=[L0|L1|L2|L3], schema_version (optional).
- Server responds with handshake frame: protocol_version, active_fidelities, chosen_schema_version, fallthrough_policy_hint.
- Frames are framed as newline-delimited messages where each message includes: frame_type(enum), frame_id, timestamp, payload (string).
- Frame types: HANDSHAKE, TEXT_DELTA, SEMANTIC_LABEL, BLOCK_STRUCT, TOOL_CALL, TOOL_RESULT, FALLTHROUGH_NOTICE, FINAL

Tool-calling semantics:
- TOOL_CALL frame (L3) contains: tool_id (string), call_id, args (JSON string), required_schema, priority.
- Server will route TOOL_CALLs to configured toolbackends (hosted tool, dedicated, or partner endpoint).
- TOOL_RESULT frame returns tool success/failure, output (typed), latency_ms, and optional evidence (trace id for the tool call).
- Tool calls may be executed synchronously (blocking the stream) or asynchronously (server emits placeholder frames and later emits TOOL_RESULT).

Tool fallthrough policy (server-driven, client-aware):
- Policies the server may choose (enumerated reasons included in FALLTHROUGH_NOTICE):
  - SOFT_FALLTHROUGH: tool timed out or rate-limited; server offers a best-effort surrogate (short summary or cached response).
  - SKIP_TOOL: tool disabled for policy/compliance; server omits action and marks candidate for manual resolution.
  - QUEUE_FOR_ASYNC: tool accepted asynchronously; client gets placeholder + eventual TOOL_RESULT via separate resume hook or webhook.
  - LOCAL_DEGRADE: model attempts to synthesize an approximation without calling the tool (lower fidelity).
- Each FALLTHROUGH_NOTICE must include: call_id, reason_code, recommended client action (retry, inform user, queue), and estimated ETA if queued.

SDK ergonomics (patterns):
Default (quickstart) path:
- rwd.client.stream({ model, prompt, fidelities: ["L0","L1"], onText: fn, onBlock: fn, onToolResult: fn })
- Callbacks are optional; absent callbacks are safe (frames are ignored).
- SDK handles reconnections and resumes using durable session ids when server supports it.

Typed path (power users):
- declarative schemas: rwd.client.streamTyped({ model, prompt, schema: { blocks: "BlockV2" }, onFrameTyped: (frame) => {} })
- SDK will validate inbound BLOCK_STRUCT/TOOL_RESULT frames against schema_version and surface structured objects or parse errors.
- Built-in helpers to auto-ack tool results and to rehydrate partial block state.

Backpressure and cancellation:
- SDK exposes backpressure hooks: onBackpressure(pressureLevel) where pressureLevel is LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH. Server may emit backpressure hints when batching or load is high.
- Client can request lower fidelity on the fly via a control frame (reduce_fidelity).
- Cancellation semantics: client can send CANCEL_FRAME to abort; server returns FINAL with status CANCELLED and best-effort final block state.

Observability and telemetry hooks:
- SDK emits events: token_latency_ms (per 128-token window), frame_receive_latency_ms, tool_call_latency_ms, tool_success_rate, schema_mismatch_count, fallthrough_count, active_fidelity_levels, session_reconnect_count.
- Recommended span tags and metrics for Redwood Console: session_id, model, fidelities, tool_id, call_id, region, chosen_capacity_tier.
- Instrumentation should include optional traces linking TOOL_CALL frames to external tool traces via trace_id.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (internal dev): implement handshake + L1 and L2 frames, SDK quickstart path, basic telemetry. Limit to internal experiments.
- Phase 1 (partner trials): enable L3 tool-call frames for selected customers and partner tool endpoints. Provide migration guide.
- Phase 2 (canary): feature flag for 10% of production calls; monitor schema_mismatch_count and fallthrough_count.
- Phase 3 (gradual rollout): 25% -> 50% -> 100% with progressive alerts and rollback windows.

Compatibility and migration notes:
- When client doesn't negotiate a handshake, server emits legacy TEXT_DELTA frames only (L0).
- Servers must include a short compatibility header for older SDKs: "compat:legacy:true".
- Schema evolution: keep a small set of stable block types (summary, code, table, action_candidate). Add new fields only in patch releases and document mapping rules.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- L3 typed actions introduce more wire size and parsing cost; should we limit L3 to dedicated/dedicated-burst capacity for initial rollout?
- How do we price asynchronous queued tool executions? bill-per-tool-call vs billed on final token output?
- Should SDK auto-retry soft fallthroughs or leave policy to app logic? (Recommend opt-in auto-retry with jitter).
- How to best surface privacy/compliance decisions (e.g., tool disabled) in a way that is machine-actionable?

Implementation notes (engineering pointers):
- Serving runtime: implement a lightweight frame router that can mark frames with session durable ids and chosen schema_version.
- Console: add a tool-call replay view and a fallthrough dashboard (reason distribution, average ETA when queued).
- SDK: provide default adapters for web (EventSource/WebSocket) and Node (ws/fetch-stream), and ensure typed parsing is safe (sandbox JSON-schema validation).

Next steps / immediate action items:
1) Product: finalize fidelity level names and minimal block types (due 2025-10-29).
2) Eng-serving-runtime: prototype handshake and smoke test with local tool emulator (due 2025-11-12).
3) Devexp/SDK: implement quickstart callbacks and telemetry hooks (due 2025-11-26).
4) Security/compliance: write short policy guide for fallthrough disclosures (due 2025-11-12).

Appendix: example small session (abridged)
- Client: stream request with fidelities: [L0,L2,L3]
- Server: HANDSHAKE{protocol_v:2, active:[L0,L2], fallthrough_hint:QUEUE_FOR_ASYNC}
- Server: TEXT_DELTA("Generating summary...")
- Server: BLOCK_STRUCT({id:100, type:"summary", text:"Top-level summary"})
- Server: TOOL_CALL({call_id:200, tool_id:"search-v1", args:{q:"recent redwood infra blog"}})
- Server: FALLTHROUGH_NOTICE({call_id:200, reason:SOFT_FALLTHROUGH, recommended:"queue"})
- Server: BLOCK_STRUCT({id:101, type:"action_candidate", title:"Open search results", candidate_tool_call_hint:200})
- Server: FINAL(status:PARTIAL, notes:"tool queued; client should listen for webhook or resume session")

This draft aims to strike a balance between developer ergonomics and production constraints. Feedback requested from eng-runtime, sdk, and privacy teams on the proposed fidelity levels and the fallthrough policy taxonomy.
